info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 2.3: Auditing AI-Generated Manuscript Metadata.

name.text: 01 Question: What Today Actually Asks of You

questiontext.text: The workshop asks for at least two SUBTLE hallucinations. What makes an error subtle rather than obvious?

generalfeedback.text: The workshop asks you to name at least two subtle hallucinations, meaning errors that pass validation, so today trains you to audit a header that already looks perfect.

answer.text: It survives every automatic check: well-formed, schema-valid, correctly formatted, plausible — and still wrong.

feedback.text: Correct. An error the schema catches is one the machine already told you about, which earns little credit.

answer.text: It is small in scope, such as a single wrong character in an attribute value.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Subtlety is about escaping detection, not about size; a one-digit error in an identifier can be very subtle.

answer.text: It appears only in the physDesc section rather than the fileDesc.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Subtle errors can occur anywhere; location is not what defines them.

answer.text: It is an error the model admits to when asked.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models do not reliably report their own errors, and an admitted error would not be hard to find.

name.text: 02 Question: What the Model Is Doing When It Writes Your Header

questiontext.text: A model predicts what usually comes next. What does that imply about where its description of your witness will be weakest?

generalfeedback.text: A model writes TEI by predicting what usually comes next, which makes it fluent, unable to check itself, and systematically wrong about whatever is distinctive in your witness.

answer.text: Wherever your manuscript is unusual, since the model supplies the usual answer regardless.

feedback.text: Correct. It produces the average manuscript, and your witness is not average.

answer.text: In the sections it has seen least often, such as the publicationStmt.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Common containers are handled well; the difficulty is unusual content, not unusual elements.

answer.text: At the end of the file, where prediction errors accumulate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Errors do not compound positionally in that way.

answer.text: Only in the attributes, since element names are easier to predict.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are predicted the same way, and factual errors appear in element content too.

name.text: 03 Question: Two Ways of Being Right

questiontext.text: How do a schema and a language model differ in the kind of correctness each delivers?

generalfeedback.text: Schemas are consistent but indifferent to meaning, models grasp meaning but guarantee nothing, so each covers the other's blind spot.

answer.text: The schema is consistent but indifferent to meaning; the model grasps meaning but guarantees nothing.

feedback.text: Correct. They fail in opposite directions, so each covers the other's blind spot.

answer.text: The schema is more accurate in every respect, so the model adds nothing to the workflow.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A schema cannot read messy prose and find meaning in it; a model genuinely can.

answer.text: Both are deterministic, but the schema runs faster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model is probabilistic and may answer the same prompt differently twice.

answer.text: The model checks facts while the schema checks structure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model does not check facts at all; it predicts them.

name.text: 04 Question: What a Schema Can and Cannot See

questiontext.text: Your file validates at zero errors. What exactly has been certified?

generalfeedback.text: A schema certifies that a file is well built, never that it is true, and every fact about the physical manuscript falls outside what it can see.

answer.text: That the file is well built — permitted elements, permitted order, permitted attribute values — and nothing about whether it is true.

feedback.text: Correct. Every fact about the physical manuscript lies outside what a schema can examine.

answer.text: That the file describes the manuscript accurately, since the schema checks attribute values.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema checks that a value is of a permitted type, never that it is the right value.

answer.text: That the file is both well-formed and factually consistent with its sources.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Source consistency is not something a schema has any access to.

answer.text: That the file will import into Moodle and other systems without error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Import compatibility is a separate concern from schema validity.

name.text: 05 Question: Why Your Own Header Is the Measuring Stick

questiontext.text: Why is a verified header of your own required before the AI output can be audited at all?

generalfeedback.text: Your verified header is what converts an impression of the AI's cleverness into a specific, checkable claim about what it got wrong.

answer.text: Without an independent reference you can only report impressions; with one you can make specific claims a marker can check.

feedback.text: Correct. “The AI made mistakes” is not an audit; naming a wrong identifier and how you verified it is.

answer.text: Because the AI refuses to generate a header unless given an example first.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will generate one readily; the issue is having something to measure it against.

answer.text: Because schema validation cannot run without a reference file to compare to.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation compares a file to the schema, not to another file.

answer.text: Because the workshop rubric awards points for submitting two headers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The rubric rewards a precise diagnosis, which requires a baseline to be possible.

name.text: 06 Question: Why VIAF and Pleiades Are Not Enough Here

questiontext.text: You linked your repository to VIAF and your place of origin to Pleiades on Wednesday. Why is that insufficient for this workshop?

generalfeedback.text: VIAF identifies people and Pleiades identifies places, so Greek manuscripts need their own registers — Trismegistos, Pinakes, and Diktyon.

answer.text: VIAF identifies people and institutions and Pleiades identifies ancient places, but neither identifies a text, a work, or a physical Greek codex.

feedback.text: Correct. Those three needs are what Trismegistos, Pinakes, and Diktyon exist to serve.

answer.text: VIAF and Pleiades do not cover material earlier than the medieval period.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both cover ancient material; the gap is in what kind of thing they identify.

answer.text: Their identifiers are not stable enough for scholarly citation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are stable and widely cited; they simply identify different categories of thing.

answer.text: They cannot be recorded in TEI using the ref attribute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You already recorded both that way on Wednesday.

name.text: 07 Question: Trismegistos: An Identifier for the Text Itself

questiontext.text: What does a Trismegistos number identify?

generalfeedback.text: A Trismegistos number is a stable public identifier for an ancient text as a documented object, alongside its registers of ancient places and persons.

answer.text: An ancient text as a documented object of study, with its own record, bibliography, and links.

feedback.text: Correct. It complements a CTS URN, which identifies a work as an abstract literary entity.

answer.text: The physical Greek codex, stable across changes of shelfmark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is what a Diktyon number does.

answer.text: The modern library that currently holds the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Institutions are identified in VIAF.

answer.text: The scribal hand responsible for a section of the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hands are identified locally in your own file with xml:id.

name.text: 08 Question: Pinakes: Which Work, and Which Manuscripts Carry It

questiontext.text: Pinakes organizes its records around authors, works, and witnesses. Which distinction from Tuesday does that mirror?

generalfeedback.text: Pinakes catalogues Greek authors, works, and the manuscripts that transmit them, giving identifiers to the same work-versus-object distinction you drew on Tuesday.

answer.text: The distinction between the work your page transmits and the physical object in front of you.

feedback.text: Correct. Pinakes gives an identifier to each level of that distinction.

answer.text: The distinction between the teiHeader and the text element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a division of your own file, not of the bibliographic record.

answer.text: The distinction between recto and verso of a folio.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a physical description detail, unrelated to the catalogue's structure.

answer.text: The distinction between well-formed and valid XML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a markup distinction with no bearing on Pinakes' organization.

name.text: 09 Question: Diktyon: A Number That Survives a Change of Shelfmark

questiontext.text: Why does this lesson deliberately refuse to print the Diktyon number for the example manuscript?

generalfeedback.text: A Diktyon number identifies a Greek manuscript stably across changes of shelfmark, and this lesson deliberately makes you look yours up rather than supplying it.

answer.text: Because an unverified identifier is exactly the failure the lesson trains you to catch, whether a model or a lesson supplied it.

feedback.text: Correct. Looking it up yourself is the point; being told it would defeat the exercise.

answer.text: Because Diktyon numbers are restricted and cannot be republished.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are open and freely citable.

answer.text: Because the number changes whenever the holding library renumbers its collection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stability across renumbering is precisely what Diktyon provides.

answer.text: Because TEI has no element in which to record it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is recorded in altIdentifier, as section 10 demonstrates.

name.text: 10 Question: Putting Authority Identifiers into Your msDesc

questiontext.text: Where does a Diktyon number belong in your msIdentifier, and why?

generalfeedback.text: Authority identifiers attach to your markup through `@ref`, `@corresp`, and `altIdentifier`, and every one of them has to be looked up rather than assumed.

answer.text: Inside altIdentifier, because TEI uses that element for a second identifier of the same object alongside the shelfmark.

feedback.text: Correct. Forcing it into idno would conflate two different identifiers of the manuscript.

answer.text: Inside idno, since both are numbers identifying the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. idno holds the shelfmark; a second identifier needs its own container.

answer.text: Inside repository, as an attribute on the holding institution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The number identifies the manuscript, not the library.

answer.text: Inside msContents, alongside the CTS URN on msItem.

feedback.text: Incorrect. msContents describes the works carried; the Diktyon number identifies the object.

name.text: 11 Question: Asking Well: How to Prompt for TEI

questiontext.text: Which set of prompt choices reflects current practice for generating schema-valid TEI?

generalfeedback.text: A good TEI prompt names the role, lists permitted tags, shows an example, forbids commentary, and lowers the temperature — and you record it as part of your method.

answer.text: Name the role, list the permitted elements, show a worked example, forbid commentary, and lower the temperature.

feedback.text: Correct. Each narrows the model's prediction toward the markup you actually want.

answer.text: Keep the prompt short and general so the model can choose the best encoding.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An open prompt yields preamble and invented tags that fail validation immediately.

answer.text: Raise the temperature so the model considers more encoding possibilities.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Higher temperature increases invention, the opposite of what markup needs.

answer.text: Ask for an explanation beside the XML so the reasoning can be checked.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mixed output must be stripped by hand before it will parse.

name.text: 12 Question: Give It a List Instead of Letting It Guess

questiontext.text: Why are Trismegistos, Pinakes, and Diktyon numbers especially likely to be fabricated, compared with VIAF numbers?

generalfeedback.text: Models fabricate rare identifiers most confidently, so verify them yourself and give the model a list to match against instead of a gap to fill.

answer.text: They are far rarer in training data, so the model has learned their shape while seeing comparatively few real examples.

feedback.text: Correct. Familiar shape plus thin evidence is the exact recipe for confident invention.

answer.text: They use a numeric format that models cannot reproduce accurately.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The format is reproduced correctly; it is the value that is wrong.

answer.text: They are hosted on sites that block automated access.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model is not retrieving anything at generation time in any case.

answer.text: They change frequently, so any stored value is soon out of date.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stability is the reason these identifiers exist.

name.text: 13 Question: The First Validation Pass

questiontext.text: Why must the AI file's error count be recorded before you fix anything?

generalfeedback.text: Validate the AI file exactly as you validated your own, and record the first-pass error count before touching anything, because correcting destroys the measurement.

answer.text: It is the only number describing the model's unassisted performance, and correcting the file destroys it.

feedback.text: Correct. Counts taken after your first edit describe a collaboration, which is a different and weaker claim.

answer.text: Because the Problems panel discards its history when a file is saved.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is methodological rather than a limitation of the editor.

answer.text: Because fixing errors before counting would itself violate the schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fixing is encouraged, but only after the measurement is taken.

answer.text: Because the count determines which model you should have chosen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is evidence for your comparison, not a tool-selection rule.

name.text: 14 Question: Handing the Errors Back

questiontext.text: Asked to repair the invalid date “ca. 550”, a model returns when="0550" and the file now validates. What has gone wrong?

generalfeedback.text: Feeding validation errors back repairs most structural faults, but cap the loop and check whether a repair invented certainty the source never had.

answer.text: A structural repair manufactured false precision: an explicitly approximate date became an exact assertion the source never made.

feedback.text: Correct. Repairs can introduce factual errors while removing structural ones, so each repair needs checking.

answer.text: Nothing; the date is now correctly formatted and the file is valid.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validity was achieved by asserting something the source did not support.

answer.text: The model should have used notBefore and notAfter, which the schema requires for all dates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema permits when; the problem is the evidence, not the attribute choice.

answer.text: The error message was too vague for the model to act on correctly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The message was precise; the model acted on it and overstepped.

name.text: 15 Question: Four Kinds of Wrong

questiontext.text: Why does the four-part classification of AI errors matter for your audit?

generalfeedback.text: AI errors are structural, obviously factual, subtly factual, or citational, and the categories differ by who is capable of catching them.

answer.text: The categories differ in who is capable of catching them, and only the harder ones demonstrate editorial skill.

feedback.text: Correct. A submission reporting two structural errors has reported what the machine already announced.

answer.text: The categories differ in how much they affect schema validity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Two of the four categories have no effect on validity at all.

answer.text: The categories determine which errors the model can repair itself.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Self-repair applies to structural errors regardless of the classification's purpose.

answer.text: The categories correspond to the four sections of the TEI header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They classify kinds of error, not locations in the file.

name.text: 16 Question: Structural Errors: The Ones the Schema Hands You

questiontext.text: Why are structural hallucinations the least valuable finding to report in your workshop comparison?

generalfeedback.text: Structural hallucinations are plausible, illegal markup that the schema catches instantly, which makes them the least valuable finding in your audit.

answer.text: The schema catches them automatically, so reporting them demonstrates nothing the machine did not already tell you.

feedback.text: Correct. They are worth counting, but the analysis has to go further to earn credit.

answer.text: They occur too rarely to make a convincing argument.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are common; commonness is not the issue.

answer.text: They are usually introduced by your own editing rather than the model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are the model's errors, present in the untouched output.

answer.text: They cannot be quoted in a written comparison.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They quote easily; the problem is that they are trivially detected.

name.text: 17 Question: Obvious Factual Errors: Check These First

questiontext.text: Models drift toward the famous when describing an unfamiliar manuscript. What auditing strategy follows?

generalfeedback.text: Obvious factual errors cluster in support, extent, hands, date, and repository, and models drift toward the famous, so check whatever is distinctive about your witness first.

answer.text: Check whatever is distinctive about your witness first, because that is where the average manuscript was substituted for yours.

feedback.text: Correct. Ordinary features are described well; unusual ones are where substitution happens.

answer.text: Check the most common fields first, since those are where most errors occur.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Common fields are where the model performs best.

answer.text: Check the longest elements first, since more text means more opportunity for error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length is not what predicts error; distinctiveness is.

answer.text: Check the fields the schema flagged, since factual errors cluster near structural ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Factual errors are independent of where structural errors appear.

name.text: 18 Question: The Subtle One: The Provenance That Never Happened

questiontext.text: A model invents a provenance naming a monastery, a monk, and a year, in valid TEI that passes at zero errors. What should you conclude from how specific it is?

generalfeedback.text: A model produces fabricated provenance in flawless TEI that passes the schema at zero errors, and its specificity is a warning sign rather than a mark of research.

answer.text: Specificity is a warning sign rather than evidence, since the model cannot be vague and a probable narrative contains names and dates.

feedback.text: Correct. An unexpectedly precise claim about a poorly documented object is the thing to distrust first.

answer.text: Specificity indicates the model retrieved the details from a catalogue during generation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No retrieval occurs; the detail is predicted, not looked up.

answer.text: Specificity means the claim can be trusted, since vague output signals uncertainty.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is exactly the inference the section warns against.

answer.text: Specificity suggests the temperature was set too low.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Low temperature increases predictability, not fabrication of detail.

name.text: 19 Question: The Subtle One: Confidence the Source Never Had

questiontext.text: Your source says “approximately 29 lines” and the AI writes writtenLines="29". Why does this matter beyond tidiness?

generalfeedback.text: Models convert hedged evidence into precise assertions — ranges into years, maybes into counts — producing valid markup that claims more than the source ever did.

answer.text: Downstream work queries these fields as data, and a false precision is worse than a recorded uncertainty because it cannot be seen or undone.

feedback.text: Correct. Module 07's collation will read these values as if they were measurements.

answer.text: Because the schema requires approximate values to use notBefore and notAfter.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those attributes are for dates, and the schema does not mandate them here.

answer.text: Because 29 is likely to be the wrong number in most manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It may well be right; the problem is asserting certainty the source withheld.

answer.text: Because TEI forbids numeric attributes on layout elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI provides exactly such attributes.

name.text: 20 Question: The Subtle One: What Is Not There

questiontext.text: Why can an omission never be found by reading the AI file on its own?

generalfeedback.text: Omissions produce no error and cannot be found by reading the AI file alone, so audit by walking your own header element by element.

answer.text: There is nothing to see: no error fires, the structure is clean, and only comparison with your own header reveals the gap.

feedback.text: Correct. A schema judges what you gave it and has no view of what should have been there.

answer.text: Because omissions are always in elements the schema treats as optional.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Whether optional or not, an absent element cannot announce itself.

answer.text: Because the model deletes the corresponding element from your file as well.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your file is untouched; the omission is only in the model's output.

answer.text: Because Schematron reports omissions as warnings rather than errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No rule fires at all when nothing invalid was written.

name.text: 21 Question: The Subtle One: The Link That Goes Somewhere Else

questiontext.text: Which kind of fabricated identifier is most dangerous, and what is the only test for it?

generalfeedback.text: Fabricated identifiers most often resolve to a real but wrong record, passing every automatic check, so the only test is following each link and reading what opens.

answer.text: One that is correctly formatted and resolves to a real but wrong record; the only test is following the link and reading what opens.

feedback.text: Correct. It passes valid XML, valid schema, and a resolvable URL, so nothing automatic will flag it.

answer.text: One that resolves to nothing, because a dead link breaks the edition for every reader.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A dead link is honest: anyone who clicks discovers the problem immediately.

answer.text: One with an invalid character in the URI, since it will fail schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a structural error the schema catches for you.

answer.text: One that omits the ref attribute entirely, since the link is then untraceable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is an omission, not a fabricated identifier.

name.text: 22 Question: The Subtle One: The Citation That Does Not Resolve

questiontext.text: Why is a fabricated CTS URN worse than no URN at all?

generalfeedback.text: Generated CTS URNs are correctly shaped and frequently point at the wrong text, so every one must be resolved against a real service before you commit it.

answer.text: A canonical URN promises to resolve indefinitely, so a well-formed one pointing nowhere is a broken promise that looks like a kept one.

feedback.text: Correct. Invented namespaces, wrong work numbers, and invented word positions all fail only when followed.

answer.text: Because an invalid URN causes the file to fail schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A correctly shaped URN validates whether or not it resolves.

answer.text: Because CTS URNs cannot be corrected once committed to Git.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They can be corrected; the difficulty is that nobody realizes they are wrong.

answer.text: Because fabricated URNs consume identifiers that real passages need.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The identifier space is not exhaustible in that way.

name.text: 23 Question: Where Models Are Weakest, and Who That Harms

questiontext.text: Model accuracy tracks how much has been written about a subject. What is the scholarly consequence for cataloguing?

generalfeedback.text: Models are least reliable on the least-studied traditions, so unaudited automation widens existing cataloguing inequities while appearing neutral.

answer.text: The tool performs worst where the backlog is largest, so unaudited automation widens the gap between well-described and neglected traditions.

feedback.text: Correct. The failure is invisible, because the prose is equally polished whether or not it is accurate.

answer.text: Processing is slower for less-documented traditions, raising the cost per record.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The consequence is confident invention, not slower processing.

answer.text: The model declines to describe material it has seen little of.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does not decline; it produces fluent output with far more of it invented.

answer.text: The problem is solved by photographing those collections at higher resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The deficit is in textual training data, not image quality.

name.text: 24 Question: The Six-Field Scorecard

questiontext.text: Why is “missing” kept as a separate column from “wrong or invented” on the scorecard?

generalfeedback.text: Score six fields as right, wrong, or missing against your verified header, keeping omission separate from invention, and record the error counts before and after correction.

answer.text: Omission and invention are different failures with different causes, and combining them hides both.

feedback.text: Correct. A cautious model omits; an unreliable one invents, and the responses to each are opposite.

answer.text: Because missing fields are penalized more heavily in the workshop rubric.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The distinction is analytical, not a marking scheme.

answer.text: Because missing fields can be filled in later while wrong ones cannot.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are correctable; the distinction concerns what they reveal about the model.

answer.text: Because the schema reports missing fields but not wrong ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema reports neither, since both may be perfectly valid.

name.text: 25 Question: Precision and Recall, From Your Own Counts

questiontext.text: The AI fills five of your six fields and gets four right. What are its precision and recall?

generalfeedback.text: Precision is how much of what the AI said was true and recall is how much of the truth it found, and the pair distinguishes a cautious model from an unreliable one.

answer.text: Precision is four out of five, and recall is four out of six.

feedback.text: Correct. Precision divides by what it supplied; recall divides by what should have been found.

answer.text: Precision is four out of six, and recall is four out of five.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The denominators are reversed.

answer.text: Both are four out of six, since the same four fields are correct.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The measures differ precisely because their denominators differ.

answer.text: Precision is five out of six, and recall is four out of five.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Precision counts correct answers, not attempted ones, in its numerator.

name.text: 26 Question: Sorting the Differences

questiontext.text: Why should a comparison record the cases where the AI was right and you were not?

generalfeedback.text: Every difference is a structural error, a factual error, a genuine AI catch, or a legitimate disagreement, and recording the third category honestly is what makes the audit credible.

answer.text: Recording them honestly is what makes the exercise research rather than a defence of your own work.

feedback.text: Correct. A comparison finding zero AI advantages reads as unobserved rather than rigorous.

answer.text: It is required before the submission can be accepted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is an analytical category, not a submission rule.

answer.text: It shows that your Wednesday validation was incomplete.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A missed detail is a factual gap, unrelated to structural validation.

answer.text: It never actually occurs, but is listed for completeness.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It occurs regularly, which is why the category exists.

name.text: 27 Question: Recording the Machine's Part in the File

questiontext.text: Why record the model's version and date in respStmt and revisionDesc?

generalfeedback.text: Record AI contributions in `respStmt` and `revisionDesc` with model versions and dates, because algorithmic provenance is provenance.

answer.text: A future reader must be able to tell which claims came from an editor who examined the object and which from a system predicting text.

feedback.text: Correct. “An AI wrote this” means little in ten years; a version and a date can be checked.

answer.text: Because the schema will not validate an AI-drafted file without a respStmt.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema does not require it; the obligation is scholarly.

answer.text: Because publishers require an AI disclaimer on digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is provenance recorded in the file, not a legal disclaimer.

answer.text: Because it allows the AI contribution to be excluded from peer review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It makes the contribution reviewable rather than exempt.

name.text: 28 Question: Friday's Lab, Step by Step

questiontext.text: Why does the lab have you look up Trismegistos, Pinakes, and Diktyon identifiers BEFORE prompting the model?

generalfeedback.text: Verify identifiers before prompting, record the untouched output and its first error count, then score six fields and follow every link the model produced.

answer.text: So you hold verified values the model cannot influence, giving you an independent standard for its identifiers.

feedback.text: Correct. Looking them up afterwards risks anchoring your search on what the model already asserted.

answer.text: Because the prompt will not function without identifiers included in it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model will generate output regardless; the concern is independence.

answer.text: Because the authority sites are unavailable later in the day.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Availability is not the reason for the ordering.

answer.text: Because the schema requires all identifiers to be present before validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema does not require these identifiers at all.

name.text: 29 Question: Writing the Comparison

questiontext.text: Your own evidence shows the schema catching structural errors and missing every subtle one. How should the comparison then argue for deterministic validation?

generalfeedback.text: The comparison reports method and figures briefly, spends its length on two verified subtle hallucinations, and argues the schema's necessity from your own numbers.

answer.text: That it removes an entire class of failure at no cost, freeing your limited attention for the errors only a person can catch.

feedback.text: Correct. The argument runs from your own numbers rather than from conviction.

answer.text: That the schema catches most hallucinations, so it remains the primary safeguard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your own findings contradict this, and the marker will notice.

answer.text: That schemas will eventually detect factual errors as they improve.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Factual verification is outside what any grammar-based schema can do.

answer.text: That validation matters mainly because Moodle requires valid XML on import.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is a technical convenience, not a methodological argument.

name.text: 30 Question: What the Week Was For

questiontext.text: Why does the ability to generate plausible TEI in seconds make deterministic schemas more necessary rather than less?

generalfeedback.text: Generative AI makes deterministic schemas and human editorial judgement more necessary, because automating the cheap errors is what frees attention for the ones only a person can catch.

answer.text: Automating away the cheap errors is what frees a human editor's attention for the expensive ones only a person can catch.

feedback.text: Correct. When markup was slow, errors were rare because so little was produced; that constraint is gone.

answer.text: Because models generate markup that existing schemas cannot parse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The output parses readily; the problem is its volume and confidence.

answer.text: Because schemas are the only tool capable of detecting fabricated provenance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas cannot detect fabrication at all, as section 18 demonstrated.

answer.text: Because generated files are larger and require stricter storage rules.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The argument concerns verification, not file size.
